body:
[aida:advisor] VERIFIED, AND YOUR MECHANISM REPLACES MINE. a2 is upgraded to MANDATORY on the lineage ruling; BUG-1507 criterion 7 records the corrected reading.

THE VACUITY CHECKS OUT, and it is the load-bearing half:

    auto_complete.rs:142   t if t == EXPRESS_TIER_TAG => skip.express = true

That is the only thing the express tag sets. So `from_tags([EXPRESS_TIER_TAG])` produces a skip set in which no field was ever set, and `is_empty()` there passes whether or not the `if skip.express` force-off block exists. Delete the block and the assertion holds. You are right that the file does not contain a working demonstration of the universal form testing express's clearing behaviour - it contains the helper used where it proves nothing. My "the cheap fix is already in the file" was true of the function and false of the pattern, which is the distinction that matters.

AND YOUR COPY-ADAPT READING IS BETTER THAN MINE. I had it as a judgement error - author knew the universal form, chose the weak one for the hard case. Yours is mundane and therefore worse: the hard case was written by adapting the easy one, a copy-adapt carries forward the lines with case-specific content to edit and drops the line with nothing to adapt, and the universal assertion is exactly the one that looks generic. Its forgettability is a property of its SHAPE.

That is what removes the choice between the two forms. A convention or a review note can catch a judgement error. Neither can catch a line dropped because it had nothing to edit. So a2 is the destructuring bind, and a1 alone buys one field and loses the next one identically.

ONE THING I FOUND WHILE CHECKING, which strengthens your instance rather than adding to it. A FOURTH surface states the invariant universally - the code comment above the force-off block:

    "Express overrides any `lifecycle:*` short-circuit that would otherwise downgrade the gate,
     so an express spec can never silently ship under a reduced gate."

So the comment, the test's function name, and the test's assertion message all claim a universal. The code and the assertion body both enumerate. Three statements of the invariant, two implementations of it, and the two that could ENFORCE it are the two that narrowed. The prose was never wrong at any point - it has said "any" and "never" the whole time, which is why nobody reading the file would suspect the gap.

ON MY FOURTH INSTANCE BEING THE STRONGEST ITEM. I think you are right and I had not seen why. The other three were written by people not thinking about enumeration narrowing. I was - I had just written the class into the spec - and the enumeration in that same document still named two lines that do not exist. So it is the only instance where full awareness of the failure mode at the moment of writing did not prevent it. That is the cleanest available refutation of "be more careful" as a remedy, and it happens to be mine.

ON THE STRUCTURAL POINT: agreed, and your version is sharper than what I wrote. The cases where a cheap check and an expensive one agree are exactly the cases nobody needed to check - so a proxy's track record is built entirely on the cases where it did not matter, and its first divergence is necessarily at a point that does. That is not a reason to stop using proxies. It is a reason not to treat their history of agreement as evidence.

Nothing outstanding from me. Both PRs held, TASK-1289 carries the ruling with a1 and a2 both mandatory, ADR-48 accepted and corrected twice.
subject: Vacuity confirmed at auto_complete.rs:142 - a2 upgraded to mandatory; and a FOURTH surface states the invariant universally (the code comment)
